\documentclass{article}
\title{Notes on Ramsey Numbers of Small Graphs}
\author{E. Fontaine}
\date{June 2026}
\begin{document}
\maketitle
\section{Introduction}
Ramsey theory asks how large a structure must be
before a prescribed substructure becomes unavoidable.
For graphs the classical question concerns two colourings of complete graphs:
no matter how the edges are coloured, a monochromatic clique of a fixed size appears
once the host graph is large enough.
The smallest host size with this property is the Ramsey number of the target cliques.

\section{A Recursive Upper Bound}
The standard argument compares the neighbourhoods of an arbitrary vertex.
If a vertex has many red neighbours, the argument recurses inside the red neighbourhood;
otherwise it recurses inside the blue neighbourhood.
Either way the two colour Ramsey number satisfies
\[
  R(s, t) \le R(s-1, t) + R(s, t-1)

  R(3, 3) = 6
\]
and the base cases on the boundary are immediate.
This recurrence already yields an exponential upper bound,
and small improvements to it are considered major results.

\section{Lower Bounds from Random Colourings}
Lower bounds come from the probabilistic method.
A uniformly random two colouring of a complete graph
avoids monochromatic cliques with positive probability
whenever the host graph is not too large.
Careful estimates of the relevant expectation
give a lower bound that grows exponentially in the clique size,
matching the upper bound up to the constant in the exponent.
Alteration arguments and local lemma refinements
push the bound slightly further in the off-diagonal regime.

\section{Small Values}
Exact values are known only in a handful of cases.
The computation of each new value mixes exhaustive search,
symmetry arguments, and a great deal of engineering.
Even the next diagonal case remains out of reach
despite decades of effort and enormous computational resources.

\section{Multicolour and Hypergraph Variants}
With more than two colours the same recursion applies,
but the resulting bounds grow considerably faster.
For hypergraphs the gap between the best bounds is even wider,
and stepping up lemmas only partially close it.
These variants are a fertile source of open problems.

\section{Remarks}
The gap between the best upper and lower bounds is still wide,
and closing it is one of the central open problems of combinatorics.
We refer the reader to the dynamic survey for the current records
and for a discussion of recent progress on diagonal numbers.
\end{document}
